entry: [[Pornography]] depicting sexual activity between men. Homoerotic art depicting men dates to many ancient civilizations. The earliest known hardcore gay film, a French production, was released in 1920. Under obscenity laws, commercially available gay material in the mid-20th century often consisted of athletic men in physique magazines, which let readers pass as fitness enthusiasts. Distribution later shifted from [[VHS]] and [[DVD]] to cable, video on demand and online sites. Its possible role in [[HIV/AIDS|HIV]] risk is contested, and many studies on the question are correlational.

City in the [[Gaza Strip]], Palestine, and capital of Gaza Governorate. It was home to Palestine's only port. Its population of 590,481 in 2017 was mostly displaced or killed in the [[Gaza war]]. Inhabited since at least the 15th century BC, it was ruled by ancient Egyptians, the [[Philistines]], Romans and [[Crusader states|Crusaders]] before the [[Ottoman Empire]] incorporated it in the 16th century. British forces took it in [[World War I]], and it became part of [[Mandatory Palestine]] in 1922. Israel occupied it in the [[Six-Day War]] in 1967. Israeli airstrikes have largely destroyed it since October 2023.

Smaller of the two Palestinian territories, with the [[West Bank]], that make up the State of [[Palestine]]. The coastal strip borders [[Egypt]], [[Israel]] and the [[Mediterranean Sea]], and covers 365 sq km. Its boundaries date from the 1949 Armistice Agreements, when Egypt controlled the area. Israel captured it in the 1967 Arab–Israeli War and withdrew its forces in 2005. The [[Oslo Accords]] created the Palestinian Authority in the mid-1990s, but [[Hamas]] took over governance in 2007 after armed conflict with Fatah. Israel and Egypt have blockaded it since 2007. In 2010 the strip had just over 2 million people, mostly Palestinian refugees and their descendants, among the most densely populated territories in the world. Since the Gaza war began in 2023, Israeli operations have caused large-scale loss of life and displacement; scholars and human-rights organizations describe them as genocide, a charge Israel denies.

Armed conflict in the [[Gaza Strip]] and Israel, from October 7, 2023. [[Hamas]] led an attack that day that killed 1,195 Israelis and foreign nationals and took 251 hostages. Over 74,000 Palestinians in Gaza have been killed since the Israeli offensive, a figure several studies in *The Lancet* consider a significant undercount. Nearly all of the strip's 2.3 million Palestinians have been forcibly displaced. Many scholars and international organizations conclude that Israel's actions constitute [[Genocide|genocide]], a charge Israel and its supporters deny. A ceasefire took effect in October 2025, but hostilities have continued.

Any of many [[Antelope|antelope]] species, most in the genus *Gazella*. Gazelles live in herds in the deserts, grasslands and [[Savanna|savannas]] of Africa, and also in southwest and central Asia and the [[Indian subcontinent]]. They are slender and fawn-colored, most standing 60–110 cm high at the shoulder. Some run in bursts of up to 100 km/h (60 mph) and sustain 50 km/h (30 mph). They eat fine, easily digested plants and leaves. Taxonomy is unsettled: *Gazella* is considered to include about 10 species, with two related genera, *Eudorcas* and *Nanger*. One species, the Queen of Sheba's gazelle, is extinct, and most surviving species are threatened to varying degrees. When threatened by predators such as [[Cheetah|cheetahs]], [[Lion|lions]] and [[Hyena|hyenas]], Thomson's gazelle performs stotting, running and jumping high before fleeing. Fossils of *Gazella* date to the [[Miocene]], around 14 million years ago.

Major city in south-central [[Turkey]], capital of Gaziantep Province. Historically known as Aintab, it is thought to occupy the site of the ancient Antiochia ad Taurum. It rose to prominence in the 14th century, was besieged by [[Timur]] in 1400, and fell to the [[Ottoman Empire]] in 1516. Its honorific prefix *Gazi* commemorates resistance to a French siege in the Franco-Turkish War. At the end of 2025 the province had 2,222,415 inhabitants, about 1.9 million of them in the urban area, making the city the fifth-most populous in Turkey. Its economy includes textiles, food processing and [[Pistachio|pistachio]] farming, and it is known for [[Baklava|baklava]]. Designated a [[UNESCO]] Creative City of Gastronomy in 2015, it was the first such city in Turkey. In the 2023 Turkey–Syria earthquake, 944 buildings collapsed in the province, and the city became a regional hub for relief work.

Port city on the Baltic coast of northern [[Poland]], capital of Pomeranian Voivodeship. First mentioned in 997, it was historically known as Danzig. It joined the [[Hanseatic League]] in the [[Middle Ages]] and was the Polish Crown's principal seaport until the early 18th century. Prussia annexed it in 1793, and it was integrated into the [[German Empire]] in 1871. It was a free city from 1807 to 1814 and again from 1920 to 1939. A military clash at Westerplatte on September 1, 1939, was one of the first events of [[World War II]]. In the 1980s Gdańsk was the birthplace of the Solidarity trade union, led by [[Lech Wałęsa]], which helped precipitate the collapse of communism in Europe. It is Poland's sixth-largest city and part of the Tricity metropolitan area, with about 1.5 million people. The city became a [[UNESCO]] City of Literature in 2025.

Rotating toothed machine part that transmits [[Torque|torque]] or rotational motion by meshing with another toothed part. Two or more meshing gears form a gear train. When a small gear drives a larger one, torque increases while rotational speed falls; the reverse happens when a large gear drives a small one, in proportion to the ratio of their tooth counts. Most vehicles use a gearbox to vary the torque applied to the wheels without changing engine speed. Gears range from a few μm in micromachines to over 10 m in mining equipment. The earliest surviving gears date to the 4th century BC in China, during the [[Warring States period]]. [[Aristotle]] described gears around 330 BC, and [[Archimedes]] greatly developed them. The [[Antikythera mechanism]], which predicted astronomical positions and [[Eclipse|eclipses]], contains the earliest surviving European gears, estimated to date from between 150 and 100 BC.

Small, mostly carnivorous [[Lizard|lizard]] of the suborder Gekkota, found on every continent except [[Antarctica]]. Geckos are the most species-rich group of lizards, with nearly 2,000 species, and range from 1.6 to 67 cm long. Most are nocturnal, and their low-light color vision is 350 times more sensitive than human eyes. Geckos other than the Eublepharidae lack eyelids; instead, a transparent membrane covers each eye, and they lick it to keep it clean. Many species have specialized toe pads that let them climb smooth vertical surfaces and cross ceilings. House geckos feed on insect pests, including [[Moth|moths]] and [[Mosquito|mosquitoes]]. The largest species, *Gigarcanum delcourti*, which was 60 cm long, is known from a single stuffed specimen in [[Marseille]], France, and was likely endemic to [[New Caledonia]]. The smallest, the Jaragua sphaero, is 16 mm long and was discovered in 2001 off [[Hispaniola]].

Grand Duke of [[Lithuania]] (r. c. 1316–41), traditionally regarded as the founder of [[Vilnius]]. His rule extended from the [[Baltic Sea]] to the [[Black Sea]], and the Gediminid dynasty he founded later ruled Poland, Hungary and [[Bohemia]]. Sources on his origins are scarce and conflicting. Facing raids by the Teutonic Knights, he allied with the [[Tatars]] in 1319 and opened talks with the [[Holy See]] for protection. He wrote to Pope John XXII and invited settlers from Hanseatic towns, offering them free access and their own laws. In 1323 he pledged to be baptized once papal legates arrived, with the support of the archbishop of [[Riga]].

American actor and founder of the Geena Davis Institute on Gender in Media. *Beetlejuice* (1988) brought her to prominence, and *The Accidental Tourist* (1988) won her the Academy Award for Best Supporting Actress. She was nominated for Best Actress for *Thelma & Louise* (1991). After the box-office failure of *Cutthroat Island* (1995), her film career declined. She later played the adoptive mother in the *Stuart Little* films and won a Golden Globe for playing the first female U.S. president in the television series *Commander in Chief*.

Semi-solid material, mostly liquid by mass, with a three-dimensional cross-linked network. Gels are defined as dilute cross-linked systems that show no flow in the steady state, though the liquid can still diffuse through them. The network gives a gel its structure, hardness and tack. Gels range from soft and weak to hard and tough. Hydrogels are [[Polymer|polymer]] networks that use water as the liquid, can contain over 90 percent water and are highly absorbent. Edible jelly is a common example. [[Colloid|Colloidal]] gels form a network of particles in a fluid and have been explored for drug release. The word was coined by Scottish chemist Thomas Graham, clipped from [[Gelatin|gelatine]].

Laboratory method for separating [[Biomolecule|biomolecules]] such as [[DNA]], [[RNA]] and [[Protein|proteins]] by size and charge. Molecules migrate through a porous gel matrix, usually agarose or polyacrylamide, under an [[Electric field]]. The gel acts as a sieve: shorter molecules move faster and farther. Proteins are separated mainly by charge in agarose, whose pores are too large to sieve them. Agarose, a [[Carbohydrate|carbohydrate]] from [[Seaweed|seaweed]], suits large DNA fragments, while polyacrylamide gives finer resolution for small DNA, RNA and proteins. DNA gel electrophoresis is usually analytical, often after [[Polymerase chain reaction|PCR]] amplification, but can also prepare samples for mass spectrometry or cloning. Stains such as ethidium bromide make the separated bands visible under ultraviolet light.

Translucent, flavorless mixture of [[Peptide|peptides]] and [[Protein|proteins]] from partial hydrolysis of animal collagen. It gels food such as jelly, gummy candy, marshmallows, [[Ice cream|ice cream]] and [[Yogurt|yogurt]], and is used in [[Medication|medications]], capsules, [[Photographic film|photographic films]] and [[Cosmetics|cosmetics]]. Gelatin is brittle when dry and rubbery when moist. Its network can hold up to 90 percent water, which suits its use in wound dressings and drug delivery. Research shows no established benefit of hydrolyzed collagen for joint health. Regulators consider the risk of disease transmission very low when standard processing methods are followed.

[[Zodiac]] constellation in the northern sky, named for the twins Castor and Pollux. It is one of the 48 constellations described by [[Ptolemy]] in the 2nd century AD and one of the 88 modern constellations. Pollux is its brightest star. Castor, the second-brightest, is a sextuple star system about 52 [[Light-year|light-years]] from Earth. Gemini lies between [[Taurus (constellation)|Taurus]] and Cancer and contains 85 naked-eye stars. It is prominent in northern winter skies. To locate it, draw a line from the [[Pleiades]] to [[Regulus]], which passes close to the ecliptic just below Castor and Pollux.

Piece of [[Mineral|mineral]] crystal, cut or polished for jewelry. Some rocks, such as [[Lapis lazuli]] and [[Obsidian]], and organic materials, such as [[Amber]] and pearl, are also used. Traditionally, emerald, ruby, sapphire and [[Diamond|diamond]] are called precious; all are very hard, rating 8 to 10 on the [[Mohs scale]]. Ruby is the red variety of [[Corundum]], and sapphire is any other color of corundum. Gemologists first identify gems by chemical composition: diamonds are carbon, while sapphires and rubies are aluminum oxide. The colored gemstone industry was estimated at US$1.55 billion in 2023 and is projected to reach $4.46 billion by 2033.

Wave of political demonstrations and uprisings led mainly by [[Generation Z]], people born from the mid-1990s to the early 2010s. The July 2024 uprising in [[Bangladesh]] is widely cited as the first successful Gen Z revolution, and a successful revolution in [[Nepal]] followed. Causes vary by country but generally involve inequality, rising living costs, [[Corruption|corruption]] and [[Authoritarianism|authoritarianism]]. Gen Z has used [[Social media]] for organizing. By 2025 and 2026 the protests had spread to Asia, Africa, Europe and Latin America. The Carnegie Endowment counted at least 120 significant anti-government protests in at least 73 countries over the year to March 2026, the most since 2017.

American actress, best known for films with her husband, director [[John Cassavetes]]. Her career in film, stage and television spanned nearly seven decades. She and Cassavetes made ten films together, including *A Woman Under the Influence* (1974) and *Gloria* (1980), both of which earned her Academy Award nominations for Best Actress. She won a Silver Bear for *Opening Night* (1977). Her other roles include *Another Woman* (1988) for [[Woody Allen]] and *The Notebook* (2004), directed by her son Nick Cassavetes. She won four Emmy Awards and two Golden Globes, and received an Honorary Academy Award in 2015.

Military or paramilitary force with law-enforcement duties among civilians. The term derives from the medieval French *gens d'armes*, or "men-at-arms," and gained policing meaning during the [[French Revolution]]. It spread to several Western European countries during [[Napoleon|Napoleon's]] conquests, and similar forces exist in most European countries. In France, the gendarmerie handles internal security mainly in rural areas and small towns, and serves as military police. Depending on the country, a gendarmerie may fall under a ministry of defense, as in [[Algeria]] and [[Poland]], or of the interior, as in [[Romania]] and [[Turkey]].

State in which people of every [[Gender|gender]] have equal ease of access to resources and opportunities. Gender equality is the goal, while gender neutrality and gender equity are practices that help achieve it. [[UNICEF]] defines it as women and men, girls and boys enjoying the same rights, resources, opportunities and protections, without requiring them to be treated identically. It is Goal 5 of the [[United Nations]] Sustainable Development Goals, and gender inequality is measured annually in the Human Development Reports. Early advocates included [[Christine de Pizan]], who argued in *The Book of the City of Ladies* (1405) that the oppression of women rested on irrational prejudice. The [[Shakers]], a celibate group, paired each male elder with a female eldress in their leadership. Debate continues over the causes of remaining gaps, such as the gender pay gap, with some analysts attributing raw differences largely to occupation, hours worked and career breaks.

American actor and novelist, a paragon of the [[New Hollywood]] movement. He enlisted in the [[United States Marine Corps]] at 16 by lying about his age, and served four and a half years as a field radio operator, stationed in China, including in [[Shanghai]]. He won Academy Awards for Best Actor for *The French Connection* (1971) and for Best Supporting Actor for *Unforgiven* (1992), in which he played a cruel sheriff in [[Clint Eastwood|Clint Eastwood's]] western. He played Lex Luthor in three Superman films. He retired from acting in 2004 and wrote novels.

American dancer, actor, singer, director and choreographer, born in [[Pittsburgh]]. Kelly sought to create a new form of American dance for the common man. He starred in, choreographed and co-directed some of the best-regarded musicals of the 1940s and 1950s. He made his film debut in *For Me and My Gal* (1942) with [[Judy Garland]]. His best-known films are *An American in Paris* (1951), which won the [[Academy Awards|Academy Award]] for Best Picture, and *[[Singin' in the Rain]]* (1952), which he co-directed and choreographed with Stanley Donen. Kelly received an Honorary Academy Award in 1952 and is credited with making ballet commercially acceptable to film audiences. He appeared in some of the last [[Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer|MGM]] musicals.

American television writer and producer, creator of [[Star Trek]]. He flew 89 combat missions in [[World War II]]. He wrote for television, including *Highway Patrol*, before creating *The Lieutenant*. *Star Trek* premiered on [[NBC]] in 1966 and ran for three seasons. He was involved in the early development of [[Star Trek: The Next Generation]], which began airing in 1987, but eased off after its first season due to ill health. In 1985 he became the first TV writer with a star on the [[Hollywood Walk of Fame]].

American stage and film actress, a leading lady of Hollywood's Golden Age. Born in [[Brooklyn]], New York, she was a 20th Century Fox contract player. She starred as Laura Hunt in *Laura* (1944), a film noir classic, and as Ellen Berent in *Leave Her to Heaven* (1945), which earned her a nomination for Best Actress. Studio co-founder Darryl F. Zanuck called her "unquestionably, the most beautiful woman in movie history." After her Hollywood career declined, she made sporadic appearances on many [[Television show|television shows]]. Her final film role was in *The Pleasure Seekers* (1964).

American actor, comedian, writer and filmmaker, known for comedies with [[Mel Brooks]] and [[Richard Pryor]]. He was nominated for Best Supporting Actor for *The Producers* (1967), the first of his collaborations with Brooks, and co-wrote *Young Frankenstein* (1974), which earned a nomination for Best Adapted Screenplay. He played Willy Wonka in *Willy Wonka & the Chocolate Factory* (1971). After his third wife, [[Gilda Radner]], died of ovarian cancer, he co-founded Gilda's Club to support cancer patients. His last acting role, on *Will & Grace* in 2003, won a Primetime Emmy; he then turned to writing.
